lessons.title: Probiotics, prebiotics and co.: definitions, strain and label
lessons.objective: Use the consensus definitions of probiotic, prebiotic, synbiotic and postbiotic, explain why evidence is strain-specific, and read a product's label, dose and safety according to WGO.
lessons.closing: Probiotic alive, postbiotic inanimate, prebiotic a substrate; all with a demonstrated benefit. Evidence is tied to the strain and its dose. Label with strain and count at the use-by date; there is no general dose. Immunocompromised: only strains with proven safety.

lessons.title: Vaginal microbiota and bacterial vaginosis
lessons.objective: Diagnose BV with Amsel, Nugent or Hay–Ison, know when not to test, treat and prevent recurrence under CDC and IUSTI, answer questions about partners and probiotics, and explain what Lactobacillus dominance does and does not mean for fertility.
lessons.closing: Amsel 3 of 4; Gram stain is the reference. Without symptoms, no routine testing (IUSTI treats BV found in some high-risk pregnant women and before invasive procedures). Metronidazole or clindamycin; recurrence: suppressive vaginal metronidazole. Male partner: do not treat. Probiotics: not supported by CDC, insufficient evidence for IUSTI. Vaginal microbiota in infertility: research only (ESHRE).

lessons.title: Endometrial microbiome, chronic endometritis and commercial tests
lessons.objective: Explain why ESHRE and NICE do not recommend endometrial microbiome profiling, where they disagree on chronic endometritis in implantation failure, and what the 2025 consensus says about commercial microbiome tests.
lessons.closing: Uterine and vaginal microbiome in RIF: not recommended (ESHRE). NICE: do not offer endometrial microbiome analysis as an add-on for any embryo transfer (silent on the vaginal microbiome). Chronic endometritis: can be considered with antibiotics in RIF (ESHRE); do not offer its analysis as a transfer add-on (NICE); no standard threshold. Stool tests: insufficient evidence for routine use and no advice from the provider.

items.title: Probiotic, prebiotic, synbiotic and postbiotic: the consensus definitions
items.core: According to the ISAPP definitions set out in its 2020 synbiotics consensus, probiotics are “live microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, confer a health benefit on the host”, and a prebiotic is “a substrate that is selectively utilized by host microorganisms conferring a health benefit”. [[ref:isapp-2020-synbiotics]] A synbiotic is “a mixture comprising live microorganisms and substrate(s) selectively utilized by host microorganisms that confers a health benefit on the host”. [[ref:isapp-2020-synbiotics]] A postbiotic is a “preparation of inanimate microorganisms and/or their components that confers a health benefit on the host”. [[ref:isapp-2021-postbiotics]]
items.body:
A synbiotic can be complementary (a probiotic plus a prebiotic, each meeting its own criteria) or synergistic (the substrate is designed to be used by the co-administered microorganism); either way the combination must show a benefit in an appropriately designed trial. [[ref:isapp-2020-synbiotics]] Postbiotics are deliberately inactivated microbial cells, with or without metabolites or cell components; purified metabolites (for example butyric acid or lactic acid) and vaccines are not postbiotics. [[ref:isapp-2021-postbiotics]]

The 2023 WGO guideline uses the same definitions of probiotic, synbiotic and postbiotic, but its definitions table keeps an older wording for prebiotic: “a selectively fermented ingredient that results in specific changes in the composition and/or activity of the gastrointestinal microbiota, thus conferring benefit(s) upon host health”. [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]] It also discourages terms such as paraprobiotic, immunobiotic or “ghost probiotic” because they lack clear definitions. [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]]
items.recall: Which word separates a postbiotic from a probiotic, and why is purified butyric acid not a postbiotic?
items.pearl: All four definitions end the same way: “confers a health benefit”. Without that demonstrated benefit, the label does not apply.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ISAPP consensus definitions (probiotic 2014, prebiotic 2017, synbiotic 2020, postbiotic 2021) taken from the definitions box of the synbiotics consensus and from the postbiotics consensus; the 2014 and 2017 papers were not read directly. WGO 2023, Table 1 (pp. 4–5). These are definitions, not graded recommendations.

items.title: The effect is shown strain by strain
items.core: For WGO 2023, the most robust way to assess a probiotic is to link each benefit to specific strains, or strain combinations, at the effective dose, and clinical recommendations should tie specific strains to the claimed benefit based on human studies. [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]] That is why the strain designation (for example, Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus GG ATCC 53103) is part of the product's identity. [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]]
items.body:
WGO describes an emerging concept: some mechanisms, such as colonisation resistance, regulation of transit or normalising a perturbed microbiota, may be shared across strains, species or even genera. [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]] Pooling different strains in a meta-analysis is valid only if a shared mechanism is shown to explain the benefit; otherwise the evidence should be strain-specific. [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]]

In 2020 the genus Lactobacillus was restructured and 23 new genera were defined: for example, Lactobacillus rhamnosus became Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus, whereas L. crispatus, L. gasseri and L. acidophilus remain in Lactobacillus. [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]]
items.recall: When does WGO accept applying the result of a mixed-strain meta-analysis to a single strain?
items.pearl: Faced with a bottle, look for the strain (the letters and numbers after the species): without it you cannot look up the evidence.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: WGO 2023, section 1 (pp. 4–8): descriptive guideline text, no recommendation grade.

items.title: Label, dose and safety of a probiotic
items.core: WGO 2023 asks that the label state genus and species (and subspecies) using current nomenclature, the strain designation, the viable count of each strain at the end of shelf-life, storage conditions, a recommended dose based on the effect, a description of the effect and a contact for post-market surveillance. [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]] There is no general dose: many products deliver 1–10 billion CFU per dose, but Bifidobacterium longum 35624 was effective in IBS at 100 million CFU/day and other products need 300–450 billion CFU three times daily. [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]]
items.body:
Because most are not made to pharmaceutical standards, regulators may not oversee their quality, and some products fail to meet label claims for the number and type of viable microbes; WGO advises reliable manufacturers that state the dose at the use-by date. [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]] What the label may claim depends on regional regulation; most are sold as foods or supplements and typically cannot mention disease. [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]]

On safety, the pathogenic potential of lactobacilli is considered quite low and bifidobacteria have a similar record, but in people with compromised immunity or serious underlying disease use should be restricted to strains and indications with proven safety and efficacy in that population. [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]]
items.recall: Which seven items should a probiotic label carry according to WGO?
items.pearl: The number that matters is the one at the use-by date, not at manufacture.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: WGO 2023, sections 2.1–2.3 (pp. 11–13): descriptive good practice, no grade. The doses quoted are the guideline's examples, not recommended regimens for gynaecological indications.

items.title: Bacterial vaginosis: a dysbiosis, often without symptoms
items.core: CDC 2021 defines bacterial vaginosis as a vaginal dysbiosis in which hydrogen peroxide- and lactic acid-producing Lactobacillus species are replaced by high concentrations of anaerobes (G. vaginalis, Prevotella, Mobiluncus, A. vaginae and others), with a polymicrobial biofilm on the epithelium. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] It is the most common cause of vaginal discharge worldwide, yet in a nationally representative survey most women with BV were asymptomatic. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]]
items.body:
IUSTI 2018 adds that it can arise and remit spontaneously and is not strictly considered a sexually transmitted infection, although it is associated with sexual activity; the G. vaginalis biofilm seems key in the switch from normal flora to BV. [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]] CDC links it to new or multiple partners, female partners, lack of condom use, douching and copper IUDs; hormonal contraception does not increase the risk and might protect, and vitamin D deficiency has not been reported as a risk factor. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]]

It is associated with higher risk of acquiring STIs (HIV, gonorrhoea, chlamydia, trichomonas, M. genitalium, HPV and HSV-2), complications after gynaecological surgery and complications of pregnancy; CDC states that all women with BV should be tested for HIV and other STIs. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]]
items.recall: What replaces Lactobacillus in BV, and what share of women with BV have no symptoms according to CDC?
items.pearl: No symptoms does not rule out BV, but, as you will see, it does not oblige you to look for it either.

evidence.label: association
evidence.note: CDC 2021, “Bacterial Vaginosis” section (narrative text; HIV/STI testing is stated as a management instruction, ungraded). IUSTI 2018, p. 2.

items.title: Diagnosing BV: Amsel, Nugent and Hay–Ison
items.core: Amsel requires at least 3 of 4 criteria: homogeneous thin discharge, clue cells on microscopy, vaginal pH > 4.5 and a fishy odour before or after adding 10% KOH. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] Gram stain is the reference method: a Nugent score of 0–3 is consistent with Lactobacillus-predominant microbiota, 4–6 with intermediate microbiota and 7–10 with BV. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]]
items.body:
Against Nugent, CDC gives Amsel a sensitivity of 37–70% and specificity of 94–99%; IUSTI quotes a sensitivity of 60–72% against Gram stain. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]] IUSTI recommends microscopy with the Hay–Ison criteria, quicker in practice, as the current best test (strength 1, quality A): grade 1 normal (lactobacilli predominate), 2 intermediate and 3 BV; grades 0 (suggests recent antibiotics) and 4 (aerobic vaginitis flora) are not related to BV. [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]]

IUSTI notes that Nugent does not take into account morphotypes not associated with BV and that “intermediate flora” has unclear clinical implications, although it is associated with complications. [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]]
items.recall: What are the four Amsel criteria, and which Nugent scores define normal, intermediate and BV?
items.pearl: A pH > 4.5 suggests BV or trichomoniasis and is almost always normal in candidiasis (IUSTI).

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: CDC 2021, “Diagnostic Considerations” (no formal grading). IUSTI 2018, pp. 3–4: Hay–Ison, strength grade 1, quality grade A (the guideline uses strength 1–2 and quality A–C; the extracted text does not include the legend for these grades).

items.title: Molecular BV panels: only with symptoms
items.core: CDC 2021 states that BV nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), which detect G. vaginalis, A. vaginae, BVAB2, Megasphaera type 1 and certain lactobacilli, should be used only in symptomatic women, because their accuracy is not well defined in asymptomatic women. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] IUSTI 2018 states that asymptomatic women do not require testing for BV, aerobic vaginitis or candida. [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]]
items.body:
Of the five quantitative multiplex assays CDC lists, two are FDA cleared and three are laboratory-developed tests that must be validated internally; traditional methods (Amsel, Nugent) remain useful because of lower cost and rapid results. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] Culture of G. vaginalis is not recommended because it is not specific, and cervical cytology has no utility for diagnosing BV. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]]

The 2025 international consensus on microbiome testing adds that multiplex PCR and cultures, although potentially useful, are not microbiome testing and cannot be used as a proxy for microbiome profiling (90% agreement), and that samples other than faeces, including vaginal swabs, should be processed according to existing scientific evidence and clinical indications (97.5%). [[ref:porcari-2025-microbiome-testing]]
items.recall: In which women does CDC accept a BV NAAT, and what does IUSTI say about asymptomatic women?
items.pearl: A “wellness” vaginal panel in a woman without symptoms has no indication in any of these sources.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: CDC 2021, “Diagnostic Considerations” (ungraded). IUSTI 2018, p. 3 (text). Porcari 2025, Table 1, statements 13 and 11 (Delphi, expert opinion; consensus threshold ≥ 80%).

items.title: Treating BV: CDC versus IUSTI
items.core: CDC 2021 recommends treating symptomatic women with metronidazole 500 mg orally twice daily for 7 days, metronidazole gel 0.75% (5 g) intravaginally once daily for 5 days or clindamycin cream 2% (5 g) intravaginally at bedtime for 7 days. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] IUSTI 2018 recommends as first line 5–7 days of oral (400–500 mg twice daily) or topical metronidazole, or 7 days of intravaginal clindamycin, depending on preference and circumstances (strength 1, quality A). [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]]
items.body:
As alternatives, CDC lists oral clindamycin or ovules, secnidazole 2 g single dose and tinidazole; IUSTI lists metronidazole 2 g single dose, tinidazole, oral clindamycin and dequalinium chloride 10 mg vaginal tablet for 6 days. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]] IUSTI notes that single-dose regimens cure less often than longer ones. [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]]

Indications differ: CDC treats symptomatic women; IUSTI adds some pregnant women with positive microscopy and a history of idiopathic preterm birth or second-trimester loss, and women undergoing gynaecological surgery or invasive diagnostic procedures, and leaves treating asymptomatic women with positive microscopy as optional. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]] CDC considers avoiding alcohol with metronidazole unnecessary and warns that clindamycin cream may weaken latex condoms and diaphragms for 5 days. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]]
items.recall: Which three regimens does CDC recommend, and in which asymptomatic situations does IUSTI treat?
items.application: In Spain, dequalinium chloride 10 mg vaginal tablets (Fluomizin) are authorised and marketed for BV. Secnidazole 2 g (Deiron) has been authorised since December 2025, but CIMA listed it as not marketed as of 14 October 2026. In Argentina, ANMAT’s national formulary includes dequalinium 10 mg pessaries (Ethopil). [[ref:aemps-2025-deiron-fluomizin]] [[ref:anmat-2026-vnm]]
items.pearl: Seven days of oral metronidazole is the regimen common to both guidelines; single dose cures less often.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: CDC 2021, “Treatment” (recommended and alternative regimens, no formal grade). IUSTI 2018, pp. 5–6: first line strength 1, quality A. The IUSTI website lists this guideline as “Under review” (accessed 14-10-2026): an update may exist that was not read.

items.title: Recurrent BV: suppression with metronidazole
items.core: After 7 days of oral metronidazole, a longitudinal study cited by IUSTI found recurrence rates of 23% at one month, 43% at 3 months and 58% at 12 months. [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]] IUSTI recommends intravaginal metronidazole as the current best treatment for persistent and recurrent BV (strength 2, quality B). [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]]
items.body:
CDC accepts repeating the same regimen or switching; with multiple recurrences, metronidazole gel 0.75% or a 750 mg metronidazole vaginal suppository twice weekly for > 3 months reduces recurrences, although the benefit does not persist once stopped. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] With limited data, it mentions an oral nitroimidazole for 7 days followed by intravaginal boric acid 600 mg daily for 21 days and metronidazole gel twice weekly for 4–6 months, and monthly oral metronidazole 2 g with fluconazole 150 mg. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]]

IUSTI also cites a small trial of intravaginal lactate gel (5 ml for 3 days after menses, for 6 months): 88% free of BV versus 10% with placebo. [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]] CDC does not recommend high-dose vitamin D to prevent recurrence and warns that douching might increase relapse. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]]
items.recall: Which treatment does IUSTI prefer for recurrent BV, and what happens when suppression stops according to CDC?
items.pearl: Suppression works while it lasts: warn that the benefit does not persist once it is stopped.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: IUSTI 2018, pp. 6–7: strength 2, quality B. CDC 2021, “Follow-Up” (ungraded text; several options with limited data).

items.title: Treat the partner? Not routinely
items.core: CDC 2021 does not recommend routine treatment of sex partners, because it does not change the woman's response or recurrence; a phase 3 trial of 7 days of oral metronidazole for male partners of women with recurrent BV did not reduce recurrence. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] IUSTI 2018 recommends that male partners do not require treatment and that female partners may be treated if they have BV (strength 2, quality B). [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]]
items.body: In women who have sex with women, partners' microbiota are often concordant: IUSTI considers it reasonable to check and treat the regular partner if she has BV, although there is no evidence that this reduces recurrence, and CDC notes that no studies have evaluated treating female partners. [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]] [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] CDC cites a pilot study in which treating the male partner (oral metronidazole plus topical clindamycin on the penis) changed the vaginal microbiota, and notes that in the phase 3 trial women whose partners adhered had fewer treatment failures; even so, it maintains that routine treatment is not recommended. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]]
items.recall: What do CDC and IUSTI say about treating male and female partners?
items.pearl: In a couple trying to conceive, treating the man “just in case” has no support from either guideline.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: CDC 2021, “Management of Sex Partners” (ungraded). IUSTI 2018, pp. 9–10: strength 2, quality B.

items.title: Probiotics for BV: the evidence falls short
items.core: CDC 2021 concludes that no studies support probiotics (intravaginal Lactobacillus or other formulations) as an adjunctive or replacement therapy for BV. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] IUSTI 2018 cites a systematic review that found insufficient evidence for or against them, and a later meta-analysis that found them effective for treating and preventing BV but with studies of variable quality; it calls for more good-quality research. [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]]
items.body:
The most promising data are still investigational: vaginal L. crispatus CTV-05 (Lactin-V), daily for 4 days in week 1 then twice weekly for 10 weeks after 5 days of metronidazole gel, substantially lowered recurrence at 12 weeks versus placebo, but according to CDC it was not FDA cleared or commercially available. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] WGO 2023, a gastroenterology guideline, mentions outside its scope that numerous studies show probiotics can reduce BV, without recommending a strain or regimen. [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]]

In short: CDC does not support probiotics for BV; IUSTI considers the evidence insufficient or of variable quality; WGO mentions them without a recommendation. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]] [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]]
items.recall: What do CDC, IUSTI and WGO say about probiotics in BV?
items.pearl: A probiotic does not replace the recommended antibiotic: according to CDC, no studies support it as a replacement or an adjunct.

evidence.label: insufficient
evidence.note: CDC 2021, “Treatment” and “Follow-Up” (text, ungraded). IUSTI 2018, p. 7 (text; no graded recommendation on probiotics). WGO 2023, p. 16 (mention outside its scope, ungraded). None of these sources assesses probiotics for fertility outcomes.

items.title: Lactobacillus dominance and fertility: what it means and what it does not
items.core: A Nugent score of 0–3 is consistent with Lactobacillus-predominant microbiota. [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] The ESHRE 2023 unexplained infertility guideline considers that vaginal microbiota testing in these couples could be considered only in a research setting (rec. 15, “research only”): evidence for a role of abnormal microbiota is insufficient and there is no evidence that correcting it improves fertility outcomes. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
The studies it reviews are case–control and cohort studies, using different detection methods (microscopy, Spiegel criteria, Nugent, qPCR), sampling at different points of the cycle or treatment, and a definition of “Lactobacillus dominance” that varies between papers. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]] The ESHRE 2023 recurrent implantation failure document notes that Lactobacillus is part of the physiological flora, but that it is unclear whether an unfavourable microbiome disrupts implantation itself or is a marker of another factor. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]]

The ESHRE 2022 recurrent pregnancy loss guideline describes an association between vaginal dysbiosis (greater diversity and lack of lactobacilli) and recurrent loss, but there are no studies on its predictive value. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.recall: What does ESHRE say about vaginal microbiota testing in unexplained infertility, and why?
items.pearl: A “low Lactobacillus” result in a woman without symptoms is not an infertility diagnosis, and ESHRE notes there is no evidence that correcting the vaginal microbiota improves fertility.

evidence.label: insufficient
evidence.note: ESHRE 2023 unexplained infertility, rec. 15 (p. 48), “Research only”; justification p. 49. ESHRE RIF 2023, “Microbiome profiling” (good practice, no GRADE). ESHRE 2022 RPL, section 1.4 (text, no recommendation).

items.title: Endometrial and vaginal microbiome profiling: not routinely
items.core: The ESHRE 2023 recurrent implantation failure document does not recommend uterine or vaginal microbiome profiling. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]] NICE NG257 (2026) advises not offering endometrial receptivity testing as a treatment add-on for embryo transfer, including microbiological analysis (for example, endometrial microbiome metagenomic analysis). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
ESHRE acknowledges associations (a meta-analysis of six cohort studies with 1,095 women, among other studies, linked dysbiotic microbiota to poorer reproductive outcomes), but lists what is missing: the optimal method of assessment, the stability and spontaneous resolution of an unfavourable microbiome, its changes during the cycle and IVF, the efficacy of interventions, and whether it is a cause or a marker. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]] In a study of 145 women with RIF and 21 controls, lactobacilli were lower in the vagina but not in the endometrium. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]]

NICE found no evidence on treating endometrial abnormalities related to the microbiome and made a research recommendation: whether treatments based on these analyses, such as antibiotics for endometritis or microbiota transplantation, improve assisted reproduction outcomes. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: What do ESHRE (RIF) and NICE NG257 say about endometrial microbiome analysis?
items.pearl: In the survey ESHRE cites, 47% of clinicians considered dysbiosis relevant in implantation failure: practice is running ahead of the evidence.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE RIF 2023, “Microbiome profiling”: red level, “not recommended” (not routinely offered; per ESHRE this does not mean forbidden in all circumstances). NICE NG257, 1.41.1 [2026] (pp. 46–47) and research recommendation 1 (p. 60).

items.title: Chronic endometritis: ESHRE allows it to be considered; NICE does not offer it as an add-on
items.core: The ESHRE 2023 recurrent implantation failure document states that assessment for chronic endometritis can be considered and, if diagnosed, antibiotic treatment can be considered. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]] NICE NG257 advises not offering microbiological analysis, including analysis of infectious chronic endometritis, as an add-on for embryo transfer. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] The ESHRE 2022 recurrent pregnancy loss guideline concludes that prospective studies and randomised trials are needed before screening for endometritis can be recommended. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.body:
It is diagnosed by hysteroscopy, haematoxylin and eosin staining and CD138 immunohistochemistry, as well as chromohysteroscopy, culture and molecular techniques, but there is no standardised plasma cell threshold (for example, > 1 or > 5 per high-power field) and studies are often small or lack controls. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]] Reviews of antibiotics conflict: one found higher live birth or ongoing pregnancy rates with cured versus persistent endometritis (OR 5.33; 95% CI 2.41–11.79), another found no significant difference (OR 2.90; 95% CI 0.65–12.98) and a third concluded that oral antibiotics did not improve pregnancy or live birth. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]]

In recurrent pregnancy loss, reported prevalence ranges from 7% to 58% depending on the method, the only study with fertile controls found no difference, and the effect of antibiotics has not been tested in randomised trials. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.recall: Where do ESHRE (RIF) and NICE disagree on chronic endometritis, and why is the antibiotic evidence conflicting?
items.pearl: If you test for it in implantation failure, agree with the patient beforehand on what you will do with the result: neither the threshold nor the antibiotic regimen is standardised in these sources.

evidence.label: limited
evidence.note: ESHRE RIF 2023, “Investigating chronic endometritis”: orange level, “can be considered” (good practice, no GRADE). NICE NG257, 1.41.1 [2026]: “do not offer”; it applies to any embryo transfer (NG257 does not specifically address recurrent implantation failure). ESHRE 2022 RPL, section 1.4: conclusion without a graded recommendation. None specifies an antibiotic regimen.

items.title: Commercial gut microbiome tests: what the 2025 consensus says
items.core: The 2025 international consensus on microbiome testing (69 experts, Delphi method) concludes that there is insufficient evidence to widely recommend routine use of these tests in clinical practice (90% agreement) and discourages patients from requesting them directly without a clinical recommendation (80.4%). [[ref:porcari-2025-microbiome-testing]] It discourages the provider from including therapeutic advice in the report (98%) and states that any change in management should be made only by the referring professional (100%). [[ref:porcari-2025-microbiome-testing]]
items.body:
On report content, it discourages the Firmicutes-to-Bacteroidetes ratio (86%), considers that there is insufficient evidence to include any dysbiosis index (90%) and that generally there is not enough information to report strict healthy reference ranges of species abundance (90%). [[ref:porcari-2025-microbiome-testing]] It also does not recommend metabolomic analysis of biofluids in clinical practice and discourages inferring the microbiome's “metabolic potential” from the taxonomic profile (90%). [[ref:porcari-2025-microbiome-testing]]

The panel warns that direct-to-consumer tests have proliferated without regulatory consensus or proven clinical value, with potential waste of resources and drawbacks in the clinical management of patients. [[ref:porcari-2025-microbiome-testing]]
items.recall: Which three elements of a commercial microbiome report does the 2025 consensus discourage?
items.pearl: If the report comes with a list of supplements or a diet, that section goes against the consensus itself.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: Porcari 2025, Table 1: statements 32, 6, 30, 3, 26, 27, 28 and 20, with their agreement rates. Expert statements (Delphi, consensus threshold ≥ 80%), not GRADE recommendations; focused on the gut microbiome.

items.stem: According to the 2021 ISAPP consensus, which of these products could be a postbiotic?

options.text: Capsules of purified butyric acid
options.why: Purified metabolites are not postbiotics; they are named by their chemical name.

options.text: A preparation of heat-inactivated lactobacilli with a demonstrated health benefit
options.why: Correct: a preparation of inanimate microorganisms and/or their components that confers a health benefit.

options.text: Capsules of live bacteria with a demonstrated benefit
options.why: If the microorganisms are alive, it is a probiotic.

options.text: Inulin selectively utilised by the microbiota with a demonstrated benefit
options.why: A selectively utilised substrate with a benefit is a prebiotic.

items.explanation: The key word is “inanimate”: a postbiotic keeps the cell (whole or as components), unlike a purified metabolite.

items.stem: A meta-analysis pools 12 different lactobacillus strains and finds a benefit. According to WGO 2023, when is it valid to apply that result to a specific strain?

options.text: Whenever the strain belongs to the same genus
options.why: Genus is not enough; WGO asks for a shared mechanism to be demonstrated.

options.text: Only if a shared mechanism is shown to explain the benefit; otherwise strain-specific evidence is needed
options.why: Correct: this is the condition WGO sets for mixed-strain meta-analyses.

options.text: If the strain is taken at more than 10 billion CFU
options.why: WGO says no general dose can be stated.

options.text: Never: WGO rejects meta-analyses with several strains
options.why: It does not reject them: they are valid if a shared mechanism is demonstrated.

items.explanation: WGO prefers linking each benefit to specific strains at the effective dose; pooling strains is valid only with a demonstrated shared mechanism.

items.stem: A woman has thin homogeneous discharge, vaginal pH 5.0 and a fishy odour on adding KOH; no microscope is available. Which statement is correct?

options.text: She meets 3 of the 4 Amsel criteria: BV can be diagnosed without microscopy
options.why: Correct: three criteria are clinical, so IUSTI accepts the diagnosis without a microscope.

options.text: Without clue cells it cannot be diagnosed
options.why: Amsel requires 3 of 4, not all 4.

options.text: A PCR panel is needed to confirm
options.why: CDC notes that traditional methods remain useful; PCR is not required.

options.text: A pH > 4.5 points to candidiasis
options.why: IUSTI states that pH > 4.5 suggests BV or trichomoniasis and is almost always normal in candidiasis.

items.explanation: Amsel: homogeneous discharge, pH > 4.5, amine odour and clue cells; 3 are enough.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman (fictional case), with no discharge, odour or itch, undergoing a fertility work-up, asks for a BV PCR panel. What best fits CDC and IUSTI?

options.text: Order it: NAATs are the reference method
options.why: The reference method is Gram stain.

options.text: It is not indicated: CDC reserves NAATs for symptomatic women and IUSTI does not indicate testing asymptomatic women
options.why: Correct: NAAT accuracy is not well defined in asymptomatic women.

options.text: Order a G. vaginalis culture
options.why: CDC does not recommend it because it is not specific.

options.text: Use cervical cytology to rule it out
options.why: According to CDC it has no clinical utility for diagnosing BV.

items.explanation: Without symptoms these guidelines do not indicate looking for BV; IUSTI only contemplates treating asymptomatic BV in some high-risk pregnant women and before invasive procedures (and as an option with positive microscopy).

items.stem: A woman with recurrent BV and a male partner asks whether her partner should be treated. What do CDC and IUSTI indicate?

options.text: Routine 7-day oral metronidazole for the man
options.why: A phase 3 trial showed no reduction in recurrence.

options.text: Do not routinely treat the male partner
options.why: Correct: CDC does not recommend it and IUSTI states he does not require treatment (strength 2, quality B).

options.text: Topical penile clindamycin plus oral metronidazole
options.why: It was only tested in a pilot study; it is not a recommendation.

options.text: Treat only if he has urinary symptoms
options.why: Neither guideline proposes that criterion.

items.explanation: Treating the male partner does not change response or recurrence; with a female partner, IUSTI accepts treating her if she has BV.

items.stem: After a BV episode treated with metronidazole, a patient wants to use a commercial vaginal probiotic instead of the antibiotic next time. Which statement fits the sources?

options.text: CDC lists it as an alternative regimen
options.why: CDC alternatives are antibiotics (clindamycin, secnidazole, tinidazole).

options.text: CDC says no studies support them as adjunct or replacement, and IUSTI considers the evidence insufficient or of variable quality
options.why: Correct: this is how both guidelines summarise it.

options.text: Lactin-V is the standard and commercially available
options.why: According to CDC it was not FDA cleared or commercially available.

options.text: IUSTI recommends them with strength 1 and quality A
options.why: IUSTI makes no graded recommendation in favour of probiotics.

items.explanation: No BV guideline supports replacing the antibiotic with a probiotic.

items.stem: Third episode of BV in a year despite recommended regimens. What does IUSTI 2018 consider the current best treatment for persistent and recurrent BV?

options.text: Intravaginal metronidazole
options.why: Correct: strength 2, quality B.

options.text: High-dose vitamin D
options.why: According to CDC, randomised trials have not shown it to reduce recurrence, and it is not recommended.

options.text: Regular vaginal douching
options.why: According to CDC they may increase relapse.

options.text: Treating the male partner
options.why: It does not reduce recurrence and is not routinely recommended.

items.explanation: CDC describes suppression with metronidazole gel twice weekly for > 3 months, with a benefit that does not persist after stopping.

items.stem: A couple with unexplained infertility asks for vaginal microbiota testing “to see whether lactobacilli are missing”. What does ESHRE 2023 say?

options.text: It is recommended for all couples
options.why: It is not part of the recommended work-up.

options.text: It could be considered only in a research setting
options.why: Correct: rec. 15, “research only”.

options.text: It is recommended if Nugent is intermediate
options.why: The guideline does not propose that indication.

options.text: It is recommended, and if lactobacilli are low, treat with probiotics
options.why: ESHRE states there is no evidence that correcting the microbiota improves fertility.

items.explanation: Heterogeneous methods, different sampling times and no evidence of benefit from correction: hence research only.

items.stem: A woman with recurrent implantation failure and a normal hysteroscopy. Regarding chronic endometritis and the endometrial microbiome, which statement is correct?

options.text: ESHRE recommends CD138 biopsy and microbiome profiling for everyone (green level)
options.why: Endometritis is “can be considered” (orange) and the microbiome “not recommended” (red).

options.text: ESHRE allows assessment for endometritis and antibiotics if diagnosed to be considered; NICE advises not offering that analysis as a transfer add-on
options.why: Correct: this is the disagreement between the two guidelines.

options.text: Both recommend endometrial microbiome profiling before the next transfer
options.why: Both advise against it: ESHRE “not recommended”, NICE “do not offer”.

options.text: There is a standardised threshold of > 5 plasma cells per field
options.why: ESHRE stresses that there is no standardised threshold (> 1 or > 5 depending on the study).

items.explanation: ESHRE (RIF): endometritis “can be considered”, microbiome “not recommended”. NICE NG257: offer neither endometrial microbiome analysis nor infectious chronic endometritis analysis as an add-on.

items.stem: A patient brings a direct-to-consumer stool test reporting an “abnormal Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio” and a supplement plan. According to the 2025 international consensus, what is correct?

options.text: The Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio is a validated dysbiosis marker
options.why: The consensus discourages reporting it (86%).

options.text: There is insufficient evidence for routine use, and the consensus discourages both that ratio and therapeutic advice from the provider
options.why: Correct: statements 32, 26 and 30.

options.text: It should be repeated monthly to follow the response to supplements
options.why: The consensus only says longitudinal assessment may be useful in specific clinical scenarios.

options.text: Before repeating it she should stop her medication and change her diet
options.why: The consensus says not to stop therapy or change diet unless the referring physician recommends it.

items.explanation: Any change in management is decided by the referring professional, not the provider.

items.title: Case: Beatriz, Federico and two microbiome tests bought online

steps.text: Beatriz (fictional case), 38, and Federico have had three transfers without implantation; their team considers that they meet ESHRE's definition of recurrent implantation failure, which uses an individual threshold of 60% cumulative predicted chance of implantation. Beatriz brings a vaginal test bought online (“low Lactobacillus”) and a direct-to-consumer stool analysis with a supplement plan. She has no discharge, odour or itch. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]]

Without symptoms, IUSTI does not indicate BV testing and CDC reserves molecular tests for symptomatic women; ESHRE does not recommend vaginal or uterine microbiome profiling in implantation failure. If microscopy showed BV, IUSTI leaves treating an asymptomatic woman as optional. [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]] [[ref:cdc-2021-sti-guidelines]] [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]]

Beatriz asks about chronic endometritis. ESHRE allows assessment and antibiotics if diagnosed to be considered, acknowledging the lack of standardisation; NICE NG257 advises not offering microbiological analysis, including infectious chronic endometritis, as a transfer add-on. You explain both positions and they decide together. If hysteroscopy with biopsy is done and BV is found, IUSTI lists women undergoing invasive diagnostic procedures among the indications for treatment. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] [[ref:iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge]]

Regarding the stool test, the 2025 international consensus considers the evidence insufficient for routine use and discourages therapeutic advice from the provider. If she still wants a probiotic, WGO asks for evidence for the specific strain; ESHRE (RIF) lists the efficacy of interventions to improve the microbiome among the unresolved questions, and the ESHRE unexplained infertility guideline notes there is no evidence that correcting the vaginal microbiota improves fertility. [[ref:porcari-2025-microbiome-testing]] [[ref:wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics]] [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]] [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

items.stem: A manufacturer sells a “synergistic synbiotic”. According to the 2020 ISAPP consensus, what distinguishes it from a complementary synbiotic?

options.text: That it contains more than one live strain, whereas the complementary one contains a single strain accompanied by any substrate
options.why: The number of strains does not define the type; what defines it is the relationship between substrate and microorganism.

options.text: That it does not need to show benefit in a trial, because the synergy between its components is assumed from laboratory studies
options.why: In both types the combination must show a benefit in an appropriately designed trial.

options.text: That its substrate is designed to be used by the co-administered microorganism
options.why: Correct: in the complementary type, probiotic and prebiotic each meet their own criteria.

options.text: That it contains heat-inactivated microorganisms together with their metabolites, which makes it both a synbiotic and a postbiotic
options.why: A synbiotic contains live microorganisms; inactivated ones fall under the postbiotic definition.

items.explanation: Per ISAPP 2020, a synbiotic can be complementary (probiotic plus prebiotic, each meeting its own criteria) or synergistic (the substrate is designed for the co-administered microorganism); either way the combination must show a benefit in an appropriately designed trial.

items.stem: A leaflet describes a product as a “paraprobiotic” or “ghost probiotic”. What does WGO 2023 say about these terms?

options.text: It discourages them because they lack a clear definition
options.why: Correct: WGO discourages paraprobiotic, immunobiotic or “ghost probiotic”.

options.text: It accepts them as official synonyms of postbiotic, so the product automatically meets the ISAPP consensus definition
options.why: WGO does not treat them as synonyms; it discourages them for lack of a clear definition.

options.text: It reserves them for products with live microorganisms that have not shown benefit, as an intermediate category before being called probiotics
options.why: The guideline creates no such category; without a demonstrated benefit, none of the consensus labels applies.

options.text: It recommends them for prebiotics, because its definition of prebiotic is based on microbiota changes and not on health benefit
options.why: Its prebiotic definition (older wording) also requires a health benefit, and these terms do not refer to prebiotics.

items.explanation: WGO 2023 uses the same definitions of probiotic, synbiotic and postbiotic as ISAPP, keeps an older wording for prebiotic (“a selectively fermented ingredient… conferring benefit(s) upon host health”) and discourages terms such as paraprobiotic, immunobiotic or “ghost probiotic” because they lack clear definitions.

items.stem: Which of these products fits the ISAPP definition of a prebiotic?

options.text: A capsule of live lactobacilli with a demonstrated benefit, because live microorganisms act as substrate for the rest of the microbiota
options.why: Live microorganisms with a demonstrated benefit fall under the probiotic definition.

options.text: A substrate selectively utilized by host microorganisms that confers a health benefit
options.why: Correct: this is the consensus definition.

options.text: Any fermentable dietary fibre, even with no demonstrated health benefit, because it is enough for the microbiota to use it
options.why: The definition requires selective utilisation and a health benefit.

options.text: A capsule of purified lactic acid, because it is a microbial metabolite that favours vaginal and gut lactobacilli
options.why: A purified metabolite is not a prebiotic, and ISAPP 2021 specifies that it is not a postbiotic either.

items.explanation: ISAPP defines a prebiotic as “a substrate that is selectively utilized by host microorganisms conferring a health benefit”. All consensus definitions require a demonstrated health benefit; purified metabolites such as lactic acid are not postbiotics.

items.stem: After the 2020 restructuring of the genus Lactobacillus reported by WGO 2023, which statement is correct?

options.text: All species moved to new genera, so the name Lactobacillus is no longer used for any species of vaginal use
options.why: L. crispatus, L. gasseri and L. acidophilus remain in Lactobacillus.

options.text: L. crispatus was renamed Lacticaseibacillus crispatus, while L. rhamnosus stayed in the genus Lactobacillus
options.why: It reverses the cases: it is L. rhamnosus that moved to Lacticaseibacillus.

options.text: The name change means that all of each strain’s previous clinical evidence is no longer valid and the trials must be repeated from scratch under the new name
options.why: The guideline describes a nomenclature change; it does not state that this invalidates prior evidence.

options.text: 23 new genera were defined: L. rhamnosus became Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus, and L. crispatus, L. gasseri and L. acidophilus remain in Lactobacillus
options.why: Correct: this is what the guideline describes.

items.explanation: In 2020 the genus Lactobacillus was restructured and 23 new genera were defined: L. rhamnosus became Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus, whereas L. crispatus, L. gasseri and L. acidophilus remain in Lactobacillus. WGO asks for labels to use current nomenclature.

items.stem: A patient brings a bottle that says only “Lactobacillus rhamnosus, 10 billion”, with no strain designation. According to WGO 2023, what is the main problem?

options.text: Without the strain designation you cannot link the product to the evidence, because benefits are attributed to specific strains at the effective dose
options.why: Correct: the strain designation is part of the product’s identity.

options.text: None, because WGO considers that all strains of a species share the same clinical effects in any indication
options.why: WGO asks for each benefit to be tied to specific strains; shared mechanisms are an emerging concept that must be shown.

options.text: That the dose is too low, because WGO sets 100 billion CFU as the minimum effective dose of any probiotic
options.why: There is no general dose: some strains are effective at 100 million CFU per day.

options.text: That the product cannot be a probiotic, because WGO requires probiotics to be manufactured to pharmaceutical standards and not sold as food supplements
options.why: WGO notes that most are not made to pharmaceutical standards, but does not require it for the definition.

items.explanation: For WGO 2023, the most robust way to assess a probiotic is to link each benefit to specific strains, or combinations, at the effective dose, based on human studies; that is why the strain designation (for example, Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus GG ATCC 53103) is part of the product’s identity.

items.stem: According to WGO 2023, at what point should the label guarantee the viable count of each strain?

options.text: At manufacture, because that is when the manufacturer can measure precisely the number of microorganisms in the pack
options.why: The count that matters is the one at the end of shelf-life.

options.text: After the pack is first opened, because from then on exposure to air and moisture reduces the number of viable bacteria
options.why: The guideline asks for the count at the end of shelf-life, together with storage conditions.

options.text: At the end of the product’s shelf-life
options.why: Correct: WGO asks for the viable count of each strain at the end of shelf-life, and for responsible manufacturers to state the dose expected at the use-by date, not at manufacture.

options.text: It need not be stated, because giving the genus and species is enough for the product to meet the probiotic definition
options.why: WGO asks for the viable count of each strain to be stated, besides the strain designation and other items.

items.explanation: WGO 2023 asks for the label to state genus and species (and subspecies) in current nomenclature, the strain designation, the viable count of each strain at the end of shelf-life, storage conditions, a recommended dose based on the effect, a description of the effect and a post-market surveillance contact; it advises reliable manufacturers that state the dose at the use-by date.

items.stem: A patient asks whether “the more CFU, the better”. What does WGO 2023 say about probiotic doses?

options.text: That the effective dose is always 1 to 10 billion CFU, and that no additional benefit has been shown above that range
options.why: Many products deliver that amount, but the guideline cites others that need 300–450 billion three times daily.

options.text: That there is no general dose: Bifidobacterium longum 35624 was effective in IBS at 100 million CFU/day and other products need 300–450 billion CFU three times daily
options.why: Correct: the dose depends on the strain and on the effect studied.

options.text: That the minimum dose for any gynaecological indication is 50 billion CFU per day for at least three months
options.why: The guideline gives no regimens for gynaecological indications; its doses are examples from other indications.

options.text: That the dose does not matter, because any number of live bacteria colonises the gut and produces the same effect
options.why: WGO asks for a recommended dose based on the effect, so the dose does matter.

items.explanation: WGO 2023 explains that there is no general dose: many products deliver 1–10 billion CFU per dose, but Bifidobacterium longum 35624 was effective in IBS at 100 million CFU/day and other products need 300–450 billion CFU three times daily. These are the guideline’s examples, not regimens for gynaecological indications.

items.stem: A woman on immunosuppressive treatment after a transplant (fictional case) wants to take a probiotic. What does WGO 2023 say about safety?

options.text: That probiotics are contraindicated in anyone who is immunocompromised, because lactobacilli have high pathogenic potential
options.why: The guideline considers the pathogenic potential of lactobacilli quite low and sets no absolute contraindication.

options.text: That no special precaution applies, because the safety record of lactobacilli and bifidobacteria is the same in any population
options.why: The guideline asks for restricted use in people who are immunocompromised or seriously ill.

options.text: That she should choose the product with the most CFU available, because a high dose offsets these patients’ weaker immune response
options.why: The guideline does not propose this; it asks for use to be limited to strains and indications with proven safety and efficacy in that population.

options.text: That, with compromised immunity or serious underlying disease, use should be restricted to strains and indications with proven safety and efficacy in that population
options.why: Correct: this is the precaution the guideline sets.

items.explanation: According to WGO 2023, the pathogenic potential of lactobacilli is considered quite low and bifidobacteria have a similar record, but in people with compromised immunity or serious underlying disease use should be restricted to strains and indications with proven safety and efficacy in that population.

items.stem: According to CDC 2021, which of these factors is associated with bacterial vaginosis?

options.text: Combined hormonal contraception, which according to CDC increases the risk by changing vaginal pH and reducing lactobacilli
options.why: CDC says the opposite: hormonal contraception does not increase the risk and might protect.

options.text: Douching and copper IUDs
options.why: Correct: both are among the associated factors, along with new or multiple partners, female partners and lack of condom use.

options.text: Vitamin D deficiency, which CDC cites as a risk factor and reason to give high-dose supplements to women with recurrences
options.why: CDC notes it has not been reported as a risk factor and does not recommend high-dose vitamin D to prevent recurrence.

options.text: Sexual abstinence, because without sexual activity lactobacilli do not receive the stimulus needed to remain dominant
options.why: The factors CDC cites are associated with sexual activity, not its absence.

items.explanation: CDC 2021 links BV to new or multiple partners, female partners, lack of condom use, douching and copper IUDs; hormonal contraception does not increase the risk and might protect, and vitamin D deficiency has not been reported as a risk factor.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman (fictional case) is diagnosed with symptomatic bacterial vaginosis. Besides treating her, what does CDC 2021 indicate?

options.text: Test her for HIV and other STIs, because BV is associated with a higher risk of acquiring them
options.why: Correct: CDC states that all women with BV should be tested for HIV and other STIs.

options.text: No further tests, because IUSTI considers that BV is not a sexually transmitted infection and therefore is not associated with other STIs
options.why: Not being strictly an STI does not prevent its association with a higher risk of acquiring STIs, and CDC asks for testing.

options.text: A Gardnerella vaginalis culture to confirm the diagnosis and cervical cytology to assess the extent of the dysbiosis
options.why: CDC does not recommend G. vaginalis culture and considers cytology of no use for diagnosing BV.

options.text: Routinely treat her male partner with 7 days of oral metronidazole to prevent recurrence and associated STIs
options.why: CDC does not recommend routine partner treatment: it does not change response or recurrence.

items.explanation: BV is associated with a higher risk of acquiring STIs (HIV, gonorrhoea, chlamydia, trichomonas, M. genitalium, HPV and HSV-2), complications after gynaecological surgery and complications of pregnancy; CDC states that all women with BV should be tested for HIV and other STIs (ungraded management instruction). IUSTI adds that it is not strictly considered an STI, although it is associated with sexual activity.

items.stem: Which statement about bacterial vaginosis is correct according to CDC 2021 and IUSTI 2018?

options.text: It always causes discharge and odour, so a woman without symptoms cannot have it and it need not be considered on examination
options.why: In a representative survey cited by CDC, most women with BV were asymptomatic.

options.text: It is an infection by a single pathogen, Gardnerella vaginalis, that is sexually transmitted and never remits without a full course of antibiotics
options.why: It is a polymicrobial dysbiosis that can arise and remit spontaneously, and is not strictly considered an STI.

options.text: It is a fungal infection diagnosed by low vaginal pH and treated in the same way as vulvovaginal candidiasis
options.why: It is a bacterial dysbiosis with pH > 4.5; candidiasis almost always has a normal pH.

options.text: It is a dysbiosis in which lactobacilli are replaced by anaerobes, the commonest cause of vaginal discharge worldwide, and often without symptoms
options.why: Correct: it summarises the CDC definition.

items.explanation: CDC 2021 defines BV as a dysbiosis in which hydrogen peroxide- and lactic acid-producing lactobacilli are replaced by high concentrations of anaerobes, with a polymicrobial biofilm; it is the commonest cause of discharge worldwide, but most women with BV in a representative survey were asymptomatic. IUSTI adds that it can arise and remit spontaneously.

items.stem: A vaginal Gram stain gives a Nugent score of 5. How is it interpreted?

options.text: Confirmed bacterial vaginosis, because any score above 3 indicates that anaerobes have already replaced the normal vaginal lactobacilli
options.why: BV corresponds to 7–10; 4–6 is intermediate microbiota.

options.text: Normal Lactobacillus-predominant microbiota, since BV is diagnosed only with a score of 9 or 10
options.why: Lactobacillus predominance corresponds to 0–3, and BV starts at 7.

options.text: Intermediate microbiota (4–6), with unclear clinical implications according to IUSTI, although it is associated with complications
options.why: Correct: 5 falls within the intermediate range.

options.text: Aerobic vaginitis flora, which according to IUSTI is unrelated to BV and corresponds to the middle score of the scale
options.why: Aerobic vaginitis flora corresponds to Hay–Ison grade 4, not to a Nugent score.

items.explanation: On the Nugent scale, 0–3 is consistent with Lactobacillus-predominant microbiota, 4–6 with intermediate microbiota and 7–10 with BV. IUSTI notes that “intermediate flora” has unclear clinical implications, although it is associated with complications.

items.stem: On microscopy with the Hay–Ison criteria, what do grades 0 and 4 mean according to IUSTI 2018?

options.text: Grade 0 suggests recent antibiotics and grade 4 aerobic vaginitis flora; neither is related to BV
options.why: Correct: IUSTI describes them this way.

options.text: Grade 0 indicates optimal normal microbiota and grade 4 severe BV, so the scale reflects the intensity of the dysbiosis
options.why: Grade 1 is normal and grade 3 is BV; 0 and 4 are unrelated to BV.

options.text: Grade 0 indicates candidiasis and grade 4 trichomoniasis, so both require culture before deciding treatment
options.why: IUSTI links grade 0 to recent antibiotics and grade 4 to aerobic vaginitis flora.

options.text: Both are equivalent to intermediate microbiota, like a Nugent score of 4–6, and are treated as mild BV
options.why: The intermediate grade is 2; grades 0 and 4 are unrelated to BV.

items.explanation: IUSTI 2018 recommends microscopy with the Hay–Ison criteria as the current best test (strength 1, quality A): grade 1 normal (lactobacilli predominate), 2 intermediate and 3 BV; grades 0 (suggests recent antibiotics) and 4 (aerobic vaginitis flora) are unrelated to BV.

items.stem: Against Gram stain (Nugent), what sensitivity and specificity does CDC 2021 give for the Amsel criteria, and what does this imply for a negative Amsel?

options.text: Sensitivity 94–99% and specificity 37–70%: a negative Amsel almost certainly rules out BV, but a positive one does not confirm it
options.why: It reverses the values: sensitivity is 37–70% and specificity 94–99%.

options.text: Sensitivity 37-70% and specificity 94-99%: a negative Amsel does not rule out BV, whereas a positive one strongly supports it (high specificity)
options.why: Correct: with moderate sensitivity, false negatives are common.

options.text: Sensitivity and specificity of 100%, because Amsel is the reference method against which the others, including Gram stain, are validated
options.why: The reference method is Gram stain, not Amsel.

options.text: Sensitivity 60–72% and specificity 10–20%, IUSTI figures showing that Amsel is useless for clinical diagnosis
options.why: IUSTI quotes a sensitivity of 60–72%, but the 10–20% specificity is wrong; CDC gives 94–99%.

items.explanation: Against Nugent, CDC gives Amsel a sensitivity of 37–70% and a specificity of 94–99%; IUSTI quotes a sensitivity of 60–72% against Gram stain. With that sensitivity, a negative Amsel does not exclude BV; with that specificity, a positive one strongly supports the diagnosis (the predictive value also depends on prevalence).

items.stem: A cervical cytology reports “flora suggestive of BV”, and a G. vaginalis culture was also requested. What does CDC 2021 say about these tests?

options.text: That G. vaginalis culture is the confirmatory test of choice and that cervical cytology is useful for screening asymptomatic women in routine practice
options.why: CDC does not recommend culture and considers cytology of no use for diagnosing BV.

options.text: That both tests replace Amsel and Nugent, because they are cheaper and faster than the traditional methods
options.why: It is Amsel and Nugent that CDC considers useful because of lower cost and rapid results.

options.text: That G. vaginalis culture is diagnostic if the count exceeds 10⁵ CFU/ml, whereas cytology needs NAAT confirmation
options.why: CDC gives no such threshold and does not recommend culture because it is not specific.

options.text: That G. vaginalis culture is not recommended because it is not specific, and that cervical cytology has no utility for diagnosing BV
options.why: Correct: this is what CDC states.

items.explanation: CDC 2021 does not recommend G. vaginalis culture because it is not specific, and considers cervical cytology of no use for diagnosing BV. Traditional methods (Amsel, Nugent) remain useful because of lower cost and rapid results.

items.stem: A laboratory offers a “vaginal multiplex PCR” marketed as a “complete microbiome study”. What does the 2025 international consensus on microbiome testing say?

options.text: That multiplex PCR is the reference method for microbiome profiling, and that cultures are obsolete for any sample
options.why: The consensus states that multiplex PCR and cultures are not microbiome testing.

options.text: That multiplex PCR and cultures, although potentially useful, are not microbiome testing and cannot be used as a proxy for microbiome profiling (90% agreement)
options.why: Correct: statement 13 of the consensus.

options.text: That vaginal samples should never be analysed, because the consensus accepts microbiome testing only on faeces
options.why: The consensus asks for non-faecal samples to be processed according to the evidence and clinical indications (97.5%), not banned.

options.text: That these tests carry a strong GRADE recommendation for screening asymptomatic women undergoing fertility work-up
options.why: The consensus is an expert Delphi, issues no GRADE recommendations, and CDC reserves BV NAATs for symptomatic women.

items.explanation: The 2025 consensus states that multiplex PCR and cultures, although potentially useful, are not microbiome testing and cannot be used as a proxy for microbiome profiling (90%), and that samples other than faeces, including vaginal swabs, should be processed according to the evidence and clinical indications (97.5%). These are Delphi statements (threshold ≥ 80%), not GRADE recommendations. This is a consensus centred on the gut microbiome; its statement 11 refers non-faecal samples to the available evidence and clinical indications.

items.stem: Which of these is one of the three CDC 2021 recommended regimens for symptomatic BV?

options.text: Metronidazole 2 g orally as a single dose, which CDC prefers for better adherence and efficacy equivalent to the 7-day regimen
options.why: The 2 g single dose is among IUSTI’s alternatives, and IUSTI notes that single-dose regimens cure less often.

options.text: Clindamycin cream 2% intravaginally once daily for 3 days, followed by a vaginal probiotic for a month to prevent recurrence
options.why: The CDC regimen is 7 days at bedtime, and CDC concludes that no studies support probiotics as adjuncts.

options.text: Metronidazole 500 mg orally twice daily for 7 days
options.why: Correct: along with metronidazole gel 0.75% for 5 days and clindamycin cream 2% for 7 days.

options.text: Fluconazole 150 mg orally as a single dose, because BV shares treatment with candidiasis in the CDC guidelines
options.why: Fluconazole appears only combined with monthly metronidazole in a suppressive option with limited data.

items.explanation: CDC 2021 recommends metronidazole 500 mg orally twice daily for 7 days, metronidazole gel 0.75% (5 g) intravaginally once daily for 5 days or clindamycin cream 2% (5 g) intravaginally at bedtime for 7 days. IUSTI includes metronidazole 2 g single dose among its alternatives and notes that single-dose regimens cure less often.

items.stem: An asymptomatic woman (fictional case) with BV-positive microscopy is about to undergo diagnostic hysteroscopy. How do IUSTI 2018 and CDC 2021 differ?

options.text: IUSTI includes women undergoing gynaecological surgery or invasive diagnostic procedures among its indications; CDC treats symptomatic women
options.why: Correct: it is one of the differences in indication between the two guidelines.

options.text: Both guidelines require treatment of any asymptomatic woman with positive microscopy, without exception, before any procedure
options.why: IUSTI leaves treating asymptomatic women with positive microscopy optional outside its specific indications, and CDC treats symptomatic women.

options.text: CDC recommends treating all asymptomatic women before any gynaecological procedure, whereas IUSTI advises against treating any woman without symptoms
options.why: It reverses the positions: it is IUSTI that adds indications in asymptomatic women.

options.text: Neither mentions asymptomatic situations, and both limit treatment to pregnant women with a history of idiopathic preterm birth or late loss
options.why: IUSTI does mention gynaecological surgery and invasive procedures, as well as some pregnant women.

items.explanation: CDC treats symptomatic women. IUSTI adds some pregnant women with positive microscopy and a history of idiopathic preterm birth or second-trimester loss, and women undergoing gynaecological surgery or invasive diagnostic procedures, and leaves treating asymptomatic women with positive microscopy as optional.

items.stem: One patient about to use vaginal clindamycin cream and another taking oral metronidazole ask about precautions. What does CDC 2021 say?

options.text: That metronidazole requires avoiding alcohol during treatment and for 72 hours afterwards, and that clindamycin cream does not interfere with barrier methods
options.why: CDC considers avoiding alcohol with metronidazole unnecessary and warns that the cream may weaken latex; 72 hours is the latex restriction after clindamycin ovules, not an alcohol rule.

options.text: That both patients must abstain from sex for a month, because both drugs damage any condom
options.why: CDC does not state this; the warning concerns clindamycin cream and latex for 5 days.

options.text: That clindamycin cream weakens only diaphragms, not condoms, and that alcohol is contraindicated with any antibiotic
options.why: The warning covers latex condoms and diaphragms, and CDC does not consider avoiding alcohol with metronidazole necessary.

options.text: That avoiding alcohol with metronidazole is unnecessary and that clindamycin cream may weaken latex condoms and diaphragms for 5 days
options.why: Correct: these are the two CDC statements.

items.explanation: CDC 2021 considers avoiding alcohol with metronidazole unnecessary and warns that clindamycin cream may weaken latex condoms and diaphragms for 5 days.

items.stem: A patient in Spain (fictional case) with bacterial vaginosis asks about dequalinium chloride and secnidazole. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Dequalinium is not authorised in Spain, whereas secnidazole 2 g (Deiron) has been marketed since December 2025 and is available in pharmacies
options.why: It reverses the situation: Fluomizin is authorised and marketed, and Deiron, authorised since December 2025, was listed as not marketed as of 14 October 2026.

options.text: IUSTI lists dequalinium 10 mg vaginal for 6 days among its alternatives; in Spain Fluomizin is authorised and marketed, and Deiron was listed as not marketed as of 14 October 2026
options.why: Correct: it matches IUSTI and the regulatory situation described.

options.text: IUSTI recommends dequalinium as first line with strength 1 and quality A, ahead of metronidazole and clindamycin
options.why: IUSTI’s first line is metronidazole or clindamycin; dequalinium is an alternative.

options.text: In Argentina dequalinium is not in ANMAT’s national formulary, so nitroimidazoles are the only local option
options.why: ANMAT’s national formulary includes dequalinium 10 mg pessaries (Ethopil).

items.explanation: IUSTI 2018 lists dequalinium chloride 10 mg vaginal for 6 days among the alternatives. In Spain, Fluomizin is authorised and marketed for BV; secnidazole 2 g (Deiron) has been authorised since December 2025, but CIMA listed it as not marketed as of 14 October 2026. In Argentina, ANMAT’s national formulary includes dequalinium 10 mg pessaries (Ethopil).

items.stem: After 7 days of oral metronidazole, which recurrence rates did the longitudinal study cited by IUSTI 2018 find?

options.text: 5% at one month, 10% at 3 months and 15% at 12 months, confirming that the 7-day regimen is usually definitive
options.why: These figures are wrong; recurrence is much higher.

options.text: 58% at one month, 43% at 3 months and 23% at 12 months, because recurrence falls as the flora recovers
options.why: It reverses the time order: cumulative recurrence rises over time.

options.text: 23% at one month, 43% at 3 months and 58% at 12 months
options.why: Correct: these are the figures cited.

options.text: 50% at one month and 100% at 12 months, so IUSTI advises against treating isolated BV episodes
options.why: The figures are wrong and IUSTI does not advise against treating episodes.

items.explanation: A longitudinal study cited by IUSTI found, after 7 days of oral metronidazole, recurrence rates of 23% at one month, 43% at 3 months and 58% at 12 months. For persistent and recurrent BV, IUSTI recommends intravaginal metronidazole as the current best treatment (strength 2, quality B).

items.stem: A woman (fictional case) with recurrent BV finishes 4 months of metronidazole gel 0.75% twice weekly with no recurrences and asks whether she is cured. What does CDC 2021 say?

options.text: That suppression for more than 3 months reduces recurrences, but the benefit does not persist once it is stopped
options.why: Correct: she should be warned that relapse may occur.

options.text: That suppression permanently eradicates the biofilm, so that after 4 months recurrence is exceptional
options.why: CDC notes that the benefit does not persist once suppression stops.

options.text: That she must continue suppression for life, because CDC considers recurrent BV an incurable chronic disease
options.why: CDC makes no such statement and does not propose indefinite suppression.

options.text: That the benefit is consolidated if she adds weekly douching, which according to CDC reduces relapses after suppression
options.why: CDC warns that douching might increase relapse.

items.explanation: With multiple recurrences, CDC 2021 notes that metronidazole gel 0.75% or a 750 mg metronidazole vaginal suppository twice weekly for more than 3 months reduces recurrences, although the benefit does not persist once stopped. It also warns that douching might increase relapse.

items.stem: On non-antibiotic measures for recurrent BV, which statement reflects the sources correctly?

options.text: CDC recommends high-dose vitamin D to prevent recurrence, and IUSTI recommends lactate gel as first line (strength 1, quality A)
options.why: CDC does not recommend high-dose vitamin D, and IUSTI only cites a small trial of lactate gel.

options.text: CDC recommends regular douching to restore pH, and IUSTI advises against any local treatment that is not an antibiotic
options.why: CDC warns that douching might increase relapse, and IUSTI cites a lactate gel trial without advising against it.

options.text: Both guidelines recommend intravaginal boric acid as sole first-line treatment instead of nitroimidazoles
options.why: CDC mentions boric acid only after an oral nitroimidazole, with limited data.

options.text: CDC does not recommend high-dose vitamin D to prevent recurrence; IUSTI cites a small lactate gel trial with 88% free of BV versus 10% with placebo
options.why: Correct: a small trial cited, not a graded recommendation.

items.explanation: CDC 2021 does not recommend high-dose vitamin D to prevent recurrence and warns that douching might increase relapse. IUSTI cites a small trial of intravaginal lactate gel (5 ml for 3 days after menses, for 6 months): 88% free of BV versus 10% with placebo. With limited data, CDC mentions an oral nitroimidazole for 7 days followed by intravaginal boric acid 600 mg daily for 21 days and metronidazole gel twice weekly for 4–6 months.

items.stem: A woman (fictional case) with BV has a regular female partner. What do IUSTI 2018 and CDC 2021 say about the partner?

options.text: Both guidelines recommend always treating the female partner, even without BV, because it is proven to reduce recurrences
options.why: IUSTI proposes treating her if she has BV, with no evidence it reduces recurrence, and CDC notes there are no studies.

options.text: Both guidelines advise against examining the female partner, because the microbiota of female partners rarely match
options.why: Female partners’ microbiota are often concordant, and IUSTI considers it reasonable to check her.

options.text: IUSTI considers it reasonable to check her and treat her if she has BV (a female partner may be treated: strength 2, quality B), with no evidence that this reduces recurrence; CDC notes no studies have evaluated it
options.why: Correct: it summarises both positions.

options.text: CDC recommends treating the female partner with 7 days of oral metronidazole based on the phase 3 trial in female partners
options.why: The phase 3 trial was in male partners, and CDC notes there are no studies on female partners.

items.explanation: IUSTI 2018 recommends that male partners do not require treatment and that female partners may be treated if they have BV (strength 2, quality B); it considers it reasonable to check and treat the regular partner, although there is no evidence that this reduces recurrence. CDC notes that no studies have evaluated treating female partners.

items.stem: In the phase 3 trial CDC cites, women whose male partners adhered to treatment had fewer failures. What does CDC 2021 conclude?

options.text: That the male partner should be treated routinely, because the adherent subgroup demonstrates a clear benefit on recurrence
options.why: Despite that finding, CDC maintains that routine treatment is not recommended.

options.text: That, despite that finding and a pilot study showing microbiota changes, routine partner treatment is not recommended
options.why: Correct: the trial did not reduce recurrence overall.

options.text: That the partner should be treated only with topical penile clindamycin, which according to the phase 3 trial was the only effective regimen
options.why: Topical clindamycin was used in a pilot study; the phase 3 trial assessed 7 days of oral metronidazole.

options.text: That treating the partner increases recurrences in the woman, so CDC expressly advises against it in any circumstance
options.why: CDC does not describe increased recurrences; the trial did not reduce them.

items.explanation: CDC 2021 does not recommend routine partner treatment: a phase 3 trial of 7 days of oral metronidazole in male partners of women with recurrent BV did not reduce recurrence, although women whose partners adhered to the regimen had fewer treatment failures. It also cites a pilot study (oral metronidazole plus topical penile clindamycin) that changed the vaginal microbiota, but maintains that routine treatment is not recommended.

items.stem: A patient reads that “Lactobacillus crispatus CTV-05 prevents BV”. What does CDC 2021 say about this product (Lactin-V)?

options.text: That it is the recommended first-line regimen for recurrent BV and can be bought over the counter in most countries
options.why: CDC states it is not yet FDA cleared or commercially available, and the trial showed lower recurrence after metronidazole, not a first-line regimen.

options.text: That it replaces metronidazole: used alone, without prior antibiotic, it cured BV in most women in the trial
options.why: In the trial it was given after 5 days of metronidazole gel, and it reduced recurrence rather than curing the episode.

options.text: That it did not reduce recurrence versus placebo, so CDC rules it out definitively and expects no further studies
options.why: It substantially lowered recurrence at 12 weeks versus placebo.

options.text: That after 5 days of metronidazole gel it substantially lowered recurrence at 12 weeks versus placebo, but was not FDA cleared or commercially available
options.why: Correct: promising data, but still not FDA cleared or commercially available.

items.explanation: According to CDC 2021, vaginal L. crispatus CTV-05 (Lactin-V), daily for 4 days in week 1 then twice weekly for 10 weeks after 5 days of metronidazole gel, substantially lowered recurrence at 12 weeks versus placebo, but was not FDA cleared or commercially available. CDC concludes that no studies support probiotics as adjunctive or replacement therapy.

items.stem: Which pairing of source and position on probiotics for BV is correct?

options.text: WGO 2023: mentions, outside its scope, that numerous studies show they can reduce BV, without recommending a strain or regimen
options.why: Correct: it is a mention without a recommendation.

options.text: CDC 2021: recommends them as an alternative to metronidazole for women who prefer to avoid antibiotics, with a specific strain
options.why: CDC concludes that no studies support them as adjunctive or replacement therapy.

options.text: IUSTI 2018: recommends them with strength 1 and quality A to prevent recurrences after each treated episode
options.why: IUSTI makes no graded recommendation: it cites insufficient or variable-quality evidence.

options.text: WGO 2023: recommends L. crispatus CTV-05 as the standard regimen for BV within its gastrointestinal indications
options.why: WGO recommends no strain or regimen for BV; CDC states that Lactin-V is not yet FDA cleared or commercially available.

items.explanation: CDC 2021 does not support probiotics for BV; IUSTI 2018 cites a systematic review with insufficient evidence for or against and a later favourable meta-analysis with studies of variable quality, and calls for more research; WGO 2023, a gastroenterology guideline, mentions them outside its scope without recommending a strain or regimen. None of these sources assesses probiotics for fertility outcomes.

items.stem: Why does ESHRE 2023 limit vaginal microbiota testing in unexplained infertility to research settings?

options.text: Because qPCR is not available outside research centres, although the evidence for its clinical usefulness is strong
options.why: The guideline does not justify it by availability; it considers the evidence insufficient.

options.text: Because randomised trials showed that correcting the microbiota worsens live birth rates in these couples
options.why: The guideline describes no such harm: it notes there is no evidence that correcting it improves outcomes.

options.text: Because evidence on the role of abnormal microbiota is insufficient, studies use different methods and definitions of “dominance”, and there is no evidence that correcting it improves fertility
options.why: Correct: this is the justification for recommendation 15.

options.text: Because ESHRE considers that the vaginal microbiota has no relationship with reproduction and advises against researching it
options.why: The guideline limits it to research, which is the opposite of advising against researching it.
