items.explanation: ESHRE 2023 on unexplained infertility considers that vaginal microbiota testing could be considered only in research (rec. 15, “research only”): evidence for a role of abnormal microbiota is insufficient and there is no evidence that correcting it improves outcomes. The studies are case–control and cohort studies, with different methods (microscopy, Spiegel criteria, Nugent, qPCR), different sampling points and variable definitions of “Lactobacillus dominance”.

items.stem: On vaginal dysbiosis in recurrent pregnancy loss and implantation failure, what do the ESHRE documents say?

options.text: That dysbiosis predicts pregnancy loss with high accuracy and that correcting it with vaginal probiotics is recommended before the next attempt to conceive is made
options.why: The 2022 guideline notes there are no studies on its predictive value and does not recommend probiotics.

options.text: The 2022 guideline describes an association with recurrent loss, with no studies on predictive value; the 2023 document is unsure whether it is a cause or a marker
options.why: Correct: association, not proven causation.

options.text: Both documents deny any association between vaginal microbiota and reproductive outcomes, and advise against researching it
options.why: Both describe associations; what is missing is evidence of causation, predictive value and efficacy of interventions.

options.text: The 2023 document states that Lactobacillus is a pathogen that disrupts implantation, so its presence should be treated with antibiotics
options.why: It states the opposite: Lactobacillus is part of the physiological flora.

items.explanation: The ESHRE 2022 recurrent pregnancy loss guideline describes an association between vaginal dysbiosis (greater diversity and lack of lactobacilli) and recurrent loss, but there are no studies on its predictive value. The ESHRE 2023 recurrent implantation failure document notes that Lactobacillus is part of the physiological flora, but it is unclear whether an unfavourable microbiome disrupts implantation itself or is a marker of another factor.

items.stem: A couple with recurrent implantation failure (fictional case) asks for endometrial microbiome metagenomic analysis before the next transfer. What do ESHRE 2023 and NICE NG257 say?

options.text: ESHRE recommends it (green level) for every couple with implantation failure, and NICE offers it after three failed transfers
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend it (red level) and NICE advises not offering it.

options.text: ESHRE forbids it in all circumstances, and NICE allows it only within publicly funded clinical trials
options.why: Per ESHRE, “not recommended” means not routinely offered, not forbidden in all circumstances.

options.text: Neither source mentions the endometrial microbiome, so there is no position on the analysis
options.why: Both mention it expressly.

options.text: ESHRE does not recommend uterine or vaginal microbiome profiling (not routinely offered), and NICE advises not offering microbiological analysis as a transfer add-on
options.why: Correct: they agree on not offering it routinely.

items.explanation: The ESHRE 2023 recurrent implantation failure document does not recommend uterine or vaginal microbiome profiling (red level; per ESHRE this does not mean forbidden in all circumstances). NICE NG257 advises not offering endometrial receptivity testing as a transfer add-on, including microbiological analysis (for example, endometrial microbiome metagenomic analysis).

items.stem: Which finding and which evidence gap do ESHRE 2023 and NICE NG257 report on the endometrial microbiome?

options.text: In 145 women with implantation failure and 21 controls, lactobacilli were lower in the vagina but not in the endometrium; NICE found no evidence on treatments and called for research
options.why: Correct: both items appear in the sources.

options.text: In 145 women with implantation failure, endometrial lactobacilli were lower than in controls, proving that their absence causes the failure
options.why: They were lower in the vagina, not the endometrium, and ESHRE is unsure whether it is a cause or a marker.

options.text: NICE reviewed several randomised trials showing that microbiota transplantation improves live births, and so recommends it in assisted reproduction
options.why: NICE found no evidence and made a research recommendation on these treatments.

options.text: The meta-analysis of six cohorts with 1,095 women showed that dysbiosis is not associated with poorer reproductive outcomes
options.why: That meta-analysis linked dysbiotic microbiota to poorer reproductive outcomes.

items.explanation: ESHRE acknowledges associations (a meta-analysis of six cohorts with 1,095 women linked dysbiotic microbiota to poorer outcomes), but in a study of 145 women with implantation failure and 21 controls lactobacilli were lower in the vagina and not in the endometrium. NICE found no evidence on treating microbiome-related endometrial abnormalities and made a research recommendation (antibiotics for endometritis or microbiota transplantation).

items.stem: Two reviews cited by ESHRE 2023 compare cured versus persistent endometritis: one gives OR 5.33 (95% CI 2.41–11.79) and the other OR 2.90 (95% CI 0.65–12.98) for live birth or ongoing pregnancy. How should they be read?

options.text: Both are significant, because both ORs exceed 1, and they show that antibiotics multiply the probability of live birth by 3–5
options.why: An OR is not a ratio of probabilities, and the second interval includes 1, so it is not significant.

options.text: Neither is significant, because both intervals are very wide, and therefore both reviews prove that antibiotics have no effect
options.why: The first interval (2.41–11.79) excludes 1; and a non-significant result does not prove absence of effect.

options.text: The first is significant (its CI excludes 1) and the second is not (its CI includes 1): the evidence is conflicting
options.why: Correct: that is why ESHRE only allows treatment to be considered.

options.text: The second is more reliable because its OR is smaller and its interval wider, which indicates a larger sample and greater precision
options.why: A wider interval indicates less precision, not more.

items.explanation: A 95% CI for an OR that excludes 1 indicates a statistically significant association: 2.41–11.79 excludes 1; 0.65–12.98 includes it. A third review concluded that oral antibiotics did not improve pregnancy or live birth. With this conflicting evidence, ESHRE 2023 allows assessment for chronic endometritis and, if diagnosed, antibiotic treatment to be considered (good practice, no GRADE).

items.stem: A woman with three pregnancy losses (fictional case) asks for a biopsy to rule out chronic endometritis. What does the ESHRE 2022 recurrent pregnancy loss guideline say?

options.text: That it recommends screening in all women with recurrent loss, with a standardised threshold of more than 5 plasma cells per field
options.why: It does not recommend screening, nor does it propose any plasma cell threshold (“more than 5 per field” is a figure from the literature that the guideline does not adopt).

options.text: That prevalence is constant at about 30% with any method and that antibiotics have been shown to reduce loss in randomised trials
options.why: Prevalence ranges from 7% to 58% depending on the method, and the effect of antibiotics has not been tested in randomised trials.

options.text: That the only study with fertile controls found twice as much endometritis in women with recurrent loss, which justifies biopsy
options.why: The only study with fertile controls found no difference.

options.text: That prospective studies and randomised trials are needed before screening for endometritis can be recommended
options.why: Correct: it is the guideline’s conclusion, without a graded recommendation.

items.explanation: The ESHRE 2022 recurrent pregnancy loss guideline concludes that prospective studies and randomised trials are needed before screening for endometritis can be recommended: reported prevalence ranges from 7% to 58% depending on the method, the only study with fertile controls found no difference and the effect of antibiotics has not been tested in randomised trials. The guideline proposes no plasma cell threshold and notes that prevalence depends on the detection method.

items.stem: A commercial gut microbiome report includes a “dysbiosis index”, “healthy” abundance ranges per species and the profile’s “metabolic potential”. What does the 2025 international consensus say?

options.text: That all three elements are validated and should be included in any quality report, provided the laboratory is accredited
options.why: The consensus considers the evidence insufficient for indices and strict ranges, and discourages inferring metabolic potential.

options.text: That there is insufficient evidence to include any dysbiosis index or, generally, strict reference ranges (90%), and it discourages inferring metabolic potential from the taxonomic profile (90%)
options.why: Correct: these are three consensus statements.

options.text: That the dysbiosis index is acceptable, but abundance ranges should be replaced by the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio
options.why: The consensus also discourages the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio (86%).

options.text: That these elements carry a weak GRADE recommendation and can be used if the clinician interprets them with the clinical picture
options.why: The consensus issues expert Delphi statements, not GRADE recommendations, and does not endorse them.

items.explanation: The 2025 consensus discourages the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio (86%), considers the evidence insufficient to include any dysbiosis index (90%) and, generally, to report strict species abundance ranges (90%), does not recommend biofluid metabolomics in clinical practice and discourages inferring “metabolic potential” from the taxonomic profile (90%). These are Delphi statements (threshold ≥ 80%), focused on the gut microbiome.

items.stem: A patient ordered a gut microbiome test herself and wants to change her treatment according to the report. What does the 2025 international consensus say?

options.text: That the patient can adjust her treatment according to the report, because the consensus encourages ordering these tests directly, without going through a health professional
options.why: The consensus discourages patients from requesting them directly without a clinical recommendation (80.4%).

options.text: That the laboratory running the test should prescribe the treatment, since it knows the results best
options.why: The consensus discourages the provider from including therapeutic advice (98%).

options.text: That it discourages ordering it without a clinical recommendation (80.4%) and that any change in management should be made only by the referring professional (100%)
options.why: Correct: these are two consensus statements.

options.text: That the consensus recommends repeating the test monthly to check the effect of treatment changes before deciding
options.why: The consensus does not recommend repeating the test monthly: it only states that longitudinal assessment may be useful in specific clinical scenarios (80%) and considers the evidence insufficient for routine use (90%).

items.explanation: The 2025 consensus (69 experts, Delphi) concludes that there is insufficient evidence to widely recommend routine use of these tests (90%), discourages patients from requesting them directly without a clinical recommendation (80.4%) and the provider from including therapeutic advice (98%), and states that any change in management should be made only by the referring professional (100%).

aemps-2025-deiron-fluomizin.title: Fichas técnicas de Fluomizin 10 mg comprimidos vaginales (cloruro de decualinio) y Deiron 2 g granulado (secnidazol)
aemps-2025-deiron-fluomizin.population: Women with bacterial vaginosis; trichomoniasis for Deiron (Spain).
aemps-2025-deiron-fluomizin.finding: Fluomizin: indicated for bacterial vaginosis; marketed. Deiron: indicated for Trichomonas vaginalis urethritis and vaginitis and for bacterial vaginosis in adults; authorised 17 December 2025; not marketed as of 14 October 2026.
aemps-2025-deiron-fluomizin.limitations: Only section 4.1 was read. Deiron: https://cima.aemps.es/cima/dochtml/ft/90874/FT_90874.html. Marketing status may change.

anmat-2026-vnm.title: Vademécum Nacional de Medicamentos (consulta pública)
anmat-2026-vnm.authors: Administración Nacional de Medicamentos, Alimentos y Tecnología Médica (ANMAT), Argentina
anmat-2026-vnm.population: Medicine presentations listed in ANMAT’s National Medicines Formulary (Argentina).
anmat-2026-vnm.finding: Listed products include: Ethopil (dequalinium chloride 10 mg pessaries; cert. 60233); Utrogestan (micronized progesterone 100 and 200 mg; cert. 40881); Visanne (dienogest 2 mg); Mirena (levonorgestrel 20 µg/24 h); cabergoline 0.5 and 1 mg; prasterone 6.5 mg pessaries; folic acid 1, 5 and 10 mg.
anmat-2026-vnm.limitations: The search shows neither indications nor package leaflets. Generic-name search is exact-match, so no results does not prove absence of registration. Only the first page of results was read.

cdc-2021-sti-guidelines.title: Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines, 2021
cdc-2021-sti-guidelines.authors: Workowski KA, Bachmann LH, Chan PA, Johnston CM, Muzny CA, Park I, Reno H, Zenilman JM, Bolan GA
cdc-2021-sti-guidelines.population: People with sexually transmitted infections or related syndromes in the USA; the bacterial vaginosis section is used here. MMWR Recomm Rep 2021;70(4):1-187.
cdc-2021-sti-guidelines.finding: BV: dysbiosis with replacement of Lactobacillus by anaerobes; mostly asymptomatic. Diagnosis by Amsel (3 of 4) or Nugent (Gram stain reference); NAATs only in symptomatic women; no G. vaginalis culture or cytology. Treat symptomatic women: oral metronidazole 7 days, metronidazole gel 5 days or clindamycin cream 7 days. Recurrence: metronidazole gel twice weekly > 3 months. Routine partner treatment not recommended. No studies support probiotics as adjunct or replacement; Lactin-V lowered recurrence in one trial but was not commercially available. High-dose vitamin D not recommended.
cdc-2021-sti-guidelines.limitations: Full text from Europe PMC (PMC8344968) read; only the BV section was used. No formal recommendation grading in the text (recommended and alternative regimens). US context; brand names and FDA clearances as of 2021.

eshre-2022-rpl.title: ESHRE guideline: recurrent pregnancy loss: an update in 2022
eshre-2022-rpl.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on RPL; Bender Atik R, Christiansen OB, Elson J, et al.
eshre-2022-rpl.population: Couples with recurrent pregnancy loss (two or more losses).
eshre-2022-rpl.finding: Low-dose folic acid has not been shown to prevent loss in unexplained RPL (strong); do not use high doses without hyperhomocysteinaemia or conditions raising NTD risk (diabetes, epilepsy). Prophylactic vitamin D may be considered in preconception counselling (GPP) although evidence of effectiveness is absent; vitamin D testing to find a cause is not recommended. Multivitamins: advise options safe in pregnancy (GPP); they are not a treatment. Sperm DNA fragmentation in couples with RPL: could be considered for diagnostic purposes, using a validated test (conditional; ⊕⊕⊕○). Parental karyotyping: not routine; can be carried out after an individual risk assessment (conditional).
eshre-2022-rpl.limitations: Recommendations table and vitamin D chapter read in the full ESHRE PDF. Specific RPL population; several recommendations are good practice points (GPP), not trial-based. Recommendations on sperm DNA fragmentation and parental karyotyping checked in the HRO summary (hoad002) and in the justification of the full PDF.

eshre-2023-rif.title: ESHRE good practice recommendations on recurrent implantation failure
eshre-2023-rif.authors: ESHRE Working Group on Recurrent Implantation Failure; Cimadomo D, de los Santos MJ, Griesinger G, Lainas G, Le Clef N, McLernon DJ, Montjean D, Toth B, Vermeulen N, Macklon N
eshre-2023-rif.population: Patients and couples undergoing IVF/ICSI with recurrent implantation failure; Hum Reprod Open 2023 (ESHRE Pages). Assumes a standard fertility work-up completed before ART.
eshre-2023-rif.finding: Defines RIF individually with a 60% threshold of cumulative predicted chance of implantation. 19 recommendations on investigations and 13 on interventions, classed as recommended, to be considered or not recommended. Recommended: review lifestyle, re-assess endometrial thickness, genetic counselling if a chromosomal abnormality is found, antiphospholipid antibodies with risk factors. To be considered: karyotyping, hysteroscopy, chronic endometritis, thyroid, PGT-A, blastocyst transfer. Not recommended: NK cells, cytokines, HLA-C, microbiome, sperm DNA fragmentation, scratching, G-CSF, intralipid, IVIG, PBMC, PRP, intrauterine hCG, heparin, GnRHa/AI pre-treatment, assisted hatching.
eshre-2023-rif.limitations: Full text read in the Europe PMC open-access XML version (PMC10270320); the PDF could not be downloaded and the colour-coded summary figures (images) were not read, only the table wording. Good practice document based on expert opinion supported by the literature and a survey, without GRADE ratings; RIF definitions vary across studies.

eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.title: Evidence-based guideline: unexplained infertility
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on Unexplained Infertility; Romualdi D, et al.
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.finding: With regular cycles, ovarian reserve testing is not required to identify the aetiology of infertility or to predict spontaneous conception over 6–12 months (strong recommendation, low certainty). IUI with ovarian stimulation first line (strong, very low certainty). ICSI not recommended over conventional IVF (rec. 42, strong, ⊕); endometrial scratching should not be offered (rec. 45, strong, ⊕⊕); adjunct oral antioxidants in women probably not recommended (rec. 46, conditional, ⊕).
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.limitations: Search up to October 2022; many recommendations with low or very low certainty. Full text read (journal summary via Europe PMC PMC10546081 and the full 114-page ESHRE guideline).

isapp-2020-synbiotics.title: The International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics (ISAPP) consensus statement on the definition and scope of synbiotics
isapp-2020-synbiotics.authors: Swanson KS, Gibson GR, Hutkins R, Reimer RA, Reid G, Verbeke K, Scott KP, Holscher HD, Azad MB, Delzenne NM, Sanders ME
isapp-2020-synbiotics.population: ISAPP expert panel (nutrition, physiology, microbiology) on the definition and scope of synbiotics; Nat Rev Gastroenterol Hepatol 2020;17(11):687-701.
isapp-2020-synbiotics.finding: Synbiotic: “a mixture comprising live microorganisms and substrate(s) selectively utilized by host microorganisms that confers a health benefit on the host”; complementary (probiotic plus prebiotic) or synergistic (substrate for the co-administered microorganism). Its definitions box also gives the ISAPP definitions of probiotic and prebiotic (“a substrate that is selectively utilized by host microorganisms conferring a health benefit”).
isapp-2020-synbiotics.limitations: Full text from Europe PMC (PMC7581511) read. Expert consensus on terminology and criteria, not a clinical guideline; it does not assess gynaecological indications. The original probiotic (2014) and prebiotic (2017) consensus papers were not read directly.

isapp-2021-postbiotics.title: The International Scientific Association of Probiotics and Prebiotics (ISAPP) consensus statement on the definition and scope of postbiotics
isapp-2021-postbiotics.authors: Salminen S, Collado MC, Endo A, Hill C, Lebeer S, Quigley EMM, Sanders ME, Shamir R, Swann JR, Szajewska H, Vinderola G
isapp-2021-postbiotics.population: ISAPP expert panel on the definition and scope of postbiotics; Nat Rev Gastroenterol Hepatol 2021;18(9):649-667.
isapp-2021-postbiotics.finding: Postbiotic: a “preparation of inanimate microorganisms and/or their components that confers a health benefit on the host”. They are deliberately inactivated microbial cells, with or without metabolites or components; purified metabolites and vaccines are not postbiotics.
isapp-2021-postbiotics.limitations: Full text from Europe PMC (PMC8387231) read. Expert consensus on terminology; it does not assess gynaecological indications. Later publisher and author corrections were not reviewed.

iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge.title: 2018 European (IUSTI/WHO) International Union against sexually transmitted infections (IUSTI) World Health Organisation (WHO) guideline on the management of vaginal discharge
iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge.authors: Sherrard J, Wilson J, Donders G, Mendling W, Jensen JS
iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge.population: Women with vaginal discharge (bacterial vaginosis, aerobic vaginitis, candidiasis and trichomoniasis) in Europe; Int J STD AIDS 2018;29(13):1258-1272.
iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge.finding: Asymptomatic women do not need BV testing. Best test: microscopy with Hay–Ison criteria (1A). First line: oral or topical metronidazole 5–7 days or intravaginal clindamycin 7 days (1A). Persistent and recurrent BV: intravaginal metronidazole (2B). Male partners: no treatment; female partners may be treated if they have BV (2B). Pregnancy: clindamycin (2C). Probiotics: a systematic review found insufficient evidence and a later meta-analysis was favourable with studies of variable quality.
iusti-2018-vaginal-discharge.limitations: Full PDF from the IUSTI website read (15 pp.). Strength “grade 1/2” and quality “grade A–C” with no legend in the extracted text. The IUSTI website lists it as “Under review” (accessed 14-10-2026); an update may exist that was not read.

nice-2026-ng257.title: Fertility problems: assessment and treatment (NG257)
nice-2026-ng257.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2026-ng257.population: People with fertility problems in the UK health system.
nice-2026-ng257.finding: Do not use AMH to predict clinical pregnancy through spontaneous conception (1.18.3). Use AMH or AFC as predictors of ovarian response to inform decisions and counselling about the likelihood of live birth after assisted conception (1.18.4). Do not use FSH as a predictor (1.18.5). Refer at presentation if the woman is 36 or over or there is a known cause or predisposing factors (1.16.8); otherwise investigation after 1 year of unprotected intercourse. Unexplained fertility problems: keep trying for 2 years in total before treatment (1.38.1); do not offer ovarian stimulation as a stand-alone treatment (1.38.2); then consider up to 4 cycles of IUI with gonadotrophins or offer IVF (1.38.3). Male factor: repeat an abnormal semen analysis, ideally at 3 months (1.17.4); do not test sperm DNA fragmentation (1.17.6); do not offer androgens (1.24.3). Endometriosis: expectant management for up to 2 years (including time already spent trying) or surgery; then consider up to 4 cycles of IUI with gonadotrophins or offer IVF (1.36.1–1.36.3). Add-ons: do not offer endometrial scratch or hysteroscopy as pre-treatment (1.40.1–1.40.2), endometrial receptivity testing (1.41.1), immunological agents (1.42.1) or PGT-A (1.48.1); do not offer assisted hatching (1.49.1, from 2004); ICSI: offer with surgically retrieved sperm or frozen–thawed oocytes, consider with abnormal semen or previous failed fertilisation, and do not use without male factor (1.50.1–1.50.5).
nice-2026-ng257.limitations: NHS (UK) context; replaces CG156. Numbering checked in the March 2026 PDF.

porcari-2025-microbiome-testing.title: International consensus statement on microbiome testing in clinical practice
porcari-2025-microbiome-testing.authors: Porcari S, Mullish BH, Asnicar F, Ng SC, Zhao L, Hansen R, O'Toole PW, Raes J, Hold G, Putignani L, et al.; Cammarota G, Gasbarrini A, Ianiro G
porcari-2025-microbiome-testing.population: Microbiome testing (mainly gut) in clinical practice; 69 experts from 18 countries, Delphi consensus. Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2025;10(2):154-167.
porcari-2025-microbiome-testing.finding: There is insufficient evidence to widely recommend routine microbiome testing (90%). It discourages direct patient requests without a clinical recommendation (80.4%), therapeutic advice from the provider (98%), the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio (86%), dysbiosis indices (90%) and strict healthy reference ranges (90%). Multiplex PCR and cultures are not microbiome testing (90%); vaginal samples should be processed according to existing evidence and indications (97.5%).
porcari-2025-microbiome-testing.limitations: The accepted author manuscript on PMC (PMC12343204) was read, not the typeset version; appendices not included. Expert-opinion statements (Delphi, ≥ 80% threshold), not GRADE recommendations; focused on the gut microbiome rather than vaginal or endometrial microbiome.

wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics.title: World Gastroenterology Organisation Global Guidelines: Probiotics and prebiotics
wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics.authors: Guarner F, Sanders ME, Szajewska H, Cohen H, Eliakim R, Herrera C, Karakan T, Merenstein D, Piscoya A, Ramakrishna B, Salminen S
wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics.population: Use of probiotics and prebiotics in gastrointestinal health and disease in adults and children; WGO global guideline (February 2023).
wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics.finding: Definitions of probiotic, prebiotic (older wording), synbiotic and postbiotic. The strongest evidence links each benefit to specific strains at the effective dose; pooling strains is valid only with a demonstrated shared mechanism. The label should state strain, viable count at end of shelf-life and an effect-based dose; there is no general dose. Some products fail label claims; safety is good in healthy people and use is restricted in the immunocompromised. Mentions, outside its scope, that probiotics can reduce bacterial vaginosis.
wgo-2023-probiotics-prebiotics.limitations: Full PDF from the WGO website read (52 pp.). Gastroenterology-focused: it does not assess probiotics for gynaecological or fertility indications. Clinical indications use Oxford 2011 levels; general sections are ungraded. A journal version exists (J Clin Gastroenterol 2024;58(6):533-553, DOI 10.1097/MCG.0000000000002002) and was not read.
